source.title: Does equivariance matter at scale?
source.authors: Johann Brehmer; S. Behrends; P. de Haan; Taco Cohen

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-law behavior in a new setting: rigid-body physics models rather than language models.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own compute-scaling fits, compute-optimal allocations, and training-data results for rigid-body prediction. Language-model scaling laws are cited as background only; the study does not test language-model cross-entropy, small-run predictions for much larger language models, or downstream task performance.
record.test_reason: The study fits Kaplan/Chinchilla-style power laws in N and D to test MSE of transformers on rigid-body physics prediction (10^16–10^19 FLOPs). It then derives compute-optimal allocations and studies scaling with repeated data. This tests whether the power-law form carries beyond text pretraining (V5) and whether exponents and the compute-optimal split depend on setup (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The paraphrase omits the authors' first conclusion: equivariance improves data efficiency, but augmentation largely closes that gap given enough epochs. It should also say the authors saw no power-law breakdown in range but make no claims about extrapolation beyond 10^19 FLOPs.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts the Kaplan/Hoffmann-style empirical scaling-law approach to rigid-body prediction, fitting test MSE against parameters and training tokens and deriving compute-optimal allocations; it is not language-model pretraining or cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state the qualitative fit is not sensitive to whether E is fitted or fixed to zero, or to the Huber-loss delta; cross-validation selected E = 0 and delta = 0.001. The compute-optimal allocation differs between the two architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Equivariant transformer reaches about 2x lower loss at every tested compute budget. Equivariance improves data efficiency, but symmetry data augmentation closes the gap given many epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural inductive bias (equivariance) shifts the scaling-law prefactor but not the compute exponent.

record.problems: Only one benchmark problem and two model families; nominal FLOPs do not map directly to wall time and throughput varies substantially; compute range stops at 10^19 FLOPs and does not establish extrapolation beyond it; the scaling ansatz does not fit perfectly, and the dataset-size scaling law was not convincing.

untested.parts: No language models or text pretraining cross-entropy.
No fit on small runs used to predict much larger runs. The authors state they cannot claim extrapolation beyond 10^19 FLOPs.
No language models. The allocation exponents for rigid-body models are recorded under V5/V7.
Depth, width and heads were tuned manually, but no loss-vs-shape results at fixed N are reported.
Only one physics benchmark and two transformer families. No image/video models, fine-tuning or transfer.
No comparison with published LM laws. No variation of schedule or dataset, and no comparison of fitting methods beyond E/δ cross-validation.

missing.what: Leave-one-out CV selected E=0 and δ=0.001. The authors state qualitative fit results are not sensitive to these fitting choices. This bears on the fitting-method part of V7, but no row records it.

Nominal FLOP throughput varies by about two orders of magnitude across model sizes and architectures (Fig. 6). Real training time at equal nominal FLOPs differs up to 10x, so the compute axis depends on how compute is counted.
missing.locator: Section 3.3 Counting FLOPs; Appendix C, Fig. 6

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 label was removed: the system is not a language model, and the power-of-compute form of N*(C) and D*(C) is a mathematical consequence of the fitted Eq. (2), not an independent test. The task loss is MSE, not cross-entropy. Neither original source is this study, so verdicts are allowed.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out pretraining cross-entropy are studied.
No test of fitting on small runs and predicting runs orders of magnitude larger; leave-one-out validation is not that test.
Tests derived compute-optimal parameter and training-token allocation for two rigid-body model families, not language models.
Does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests rigid-body physics prediction and data augmentation, not image/video models, fine-tuning, transfer, or other listed regimes.
No downstream task performance is measured.
Compares two architectures and reports fit sensitivity to selected fitting choices, but does not compare published language-model exponents or systematically vary data and training schedules.

rows.subject: Baseline transformer
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of unique training tokens at fixed compute, model size, and training-token budget.
rows.measure: Test loss versus unique training dataset size.
rows.note: The authors say they did not find a scaling law that convincingly describes scaling with training dataset size; they do not specify a functional form.
rows.check: Loss does improve with unique data in Fig. 2, but no power law (including Muennighoff's data-constrained law) fit convincingly. For the repeated-data regime of V5 this is a partial result, not absence of any effect.

rows.subject: Baseline transformer trained with data augmentation
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of unique training tokens at fixed compute, model size, and training-token budget; apply symmetry transformations independently each epoch.

rows.note: The authors say they did not find a scaling law that convincingly describes scaling with training dataset size. Text states augmentation makes the baseline as data-efficient as the equivariant model when the number of epochs is sufficiently large.
rows.check: Same as r7. The augmentation comparison itself (closing the gap to the equivariant model) bears on no version.

relationships.display_finding: Parameter-and-data power laws fitted both architectures well, with derived compute-scaling exponents of 0.268 and 0.236.
